images.text:
Vanessa: Peter! You put so much sugar in your coffee! And, do you use cream?
Peter: Yes, I always order double-double.
Vanessa: You know what people say, “You are what you eat”, right?
Peter: Yes, I know. If I eat unhealthy food, I'll be unhealthy. Junk in, junk out. It's just a habit. I'm so used to putting sugar in that I just do it automatically. Amy said that I was already sweet enough, so I don't need more sugar.

Vanessa: Anyway, you really should try to cut down on fat and refined sugar. White sugar is such a damaging ingredient that some people consider it a poison.
Peter: A poison? Really?
Vanessa: It's very bad for you. My doctor warned me that it can cause cancer. Cancer feeds on sugar. We get sugar from fruit and other foods so we shouldn't add more in the form of refined sugar.

Peter: That sounds pretty serious. I don't think much about sugar. My doctor told me that I have to cut down on fat. I've been trying to eat less fried food but again, it's just a habit.
Vanessa: Have you ever thought about doing a cleanse? A friend of mine did one and she said it totally changed her eating habits. It changed her diet in such a way that she doesn't have the cravings that she used to.
Peter: What's a cleanse?

Vanessa: You have to cut out sugar, fat, starch, dairy, alcohol, caffeine and sometimes meat for a specific period. Most people do it for a month.
Peter: A month? I'm not sure I could do it for a day! I'm so addicted to caffeine that I have to have at least two coffees a day, or I'm jonesing.
Vanessa: Yes. That's the point. You need to break your addictions. It takes a while for your body to get used to not having it every day. I think you should try it.

The Result Clause
You can use a result clause in your sentence to show the result of a situation. A result is something that happens because of something else that happened before.
I'm so used to putting sugar in that I just do it automatically.
Result clauses can be expressed by using:
so … or so … that
This comes at the start of the result clause and also before adjectives or adverbs. When you use so before adjectives or adverbs, you can use that after it.

Example:
She needed some more money, so she applied for another job.
I was so frustrated that I almost hit someone.
The next sentence is more formal, but you can use the so at the beginning of the sentence.

Example:
So frustrated was I that I almost hit someone.

 If you omit that, you need a comma in its place.

Example:
So frustrated was I, I almost hit someone.
such … (that)

You can use such before a noun followed by that. You can use such with or without an adjective.
You can omit that.

Examples:
It was such an enjoyable wedding that most of the guests left after midnight.
The couple showed such honesty and happiness while saying their wedding vows that most of the guests cried.
in such a way that or in such a way as to
You use this to show the result of the verb that comes before it. In other words, "with the result that".

Example:
The president spoke in such a way that everyone could understand him.
(Everyone could understand the president because of how he spoke to them.)
He played the violin in such a way as to leave the audience speechless.
(Leaving the audience speechless is the result of him playing the violin in a certain way.)
White sugar is such a damaging ingredient that some people consider it a poison.
It changed her diet in such a way that she doesn't have the cravings that she used to.
I'm so addicted to caffeine that I have to have at least two coffees a day, or I'm jonesing.
Reporting Other People's Words and Thoughts
You can report what other people say or think by using your own words or by quoting them exactly.
You know that people say, “You are what you eat,” right?
If you are talking to someone and want to relay what another person said or thought, you can use a reporting verb (say, tell, explain, etc.) and a reported clause.
The reporting clause explains who said something (the speaker) and the reported clause is what he/she said.

Examples:
Laura said (that) she was going to study psychology abroad.
He complained about how expensive it was to live in the city.
In the examples above, you are using your own words to report what someone else said. The words in bold are the reporting clause. The underlined parts are the reported clauses.
If you want to report exactly what was said, however, you will need to use quotation marks.

Examples:
"It is expensive to live in the city," he complained.
Laura said, "I'm going to study psychology abroad."
"Unfortunately," Laura admitted, "I will miss my family."
The reporting clause (in bold) can come before, after or within the quotation.
What about the following examples?

“I'm going to study psychology abroad,” said Laura.
“I'm going to study psychology abroad,” she said.
Did you notice the difference?
If the reporting clause comes after what is said (the quotation), the reporting verb usually goes before the subject. If the subject is a pronoun, the reporting verb goes after.
